<math>[\wp(z)-e_1]^{\frac{1}{2}}</math>, if we attach a definite sign to it for some particular value of <math>z</math>, is a single valued function of <math>z</math>; for it can at most have two values, and the only small circuits in the plane which could lead to an interchange of these values are those about either a pole or a zero, neither of which, as we have seen, has this effect; the function is therefore single valued for any circuit. Denoting the function, for a moment, by <math>f_1(z)</math>, we have <math>f_1(z+\omega) = \pm f_1(z)</math>, <math>f_1(z+\omega') = \pm f_1(z)</math>; it can be seen by considerations of continuity that the right sign in either of these equations does not vary with <math>z</math>; not both these signs can be positive, since the function has only one pole, of the first order, in a parallelogram <math>(\omega, \omega')</math>; from the expansion of <math>f_1(z)</math> about <math>z=0</math>, namely <math>z^{-1}(1-\tfrac{1}{2}e_1z^2+\dots)</math>, it follows that <math>f_1(z)</math> is an odd function, and hence <math>f_1(-\tfrac{1}{2}\omega') = -f_1(\tfrac{1}{2}\omega')</math>, which is not zero since <math>[f_1(\tfrac{1}{2}\omega')]^2 = e_3-e_1</math>, so that we have <math>f_1(z+\omega') = -f_1(z)</math>; an equation <math>f_1(z+\omega) = -f_1(z)</math> would then give <math>f_1(z+\omega+\omega') = f_1(z)</math>, and hence <math>f_1(\tfrac{1}{2}\omega+\tfrac{1}{2}\omega') = f_1(-\tfrac{1}{2}\omega-\tfrac{1}{2}\omega')</math>, of which the latter is <math>-f_1(\tfrac{1}{2}\omega+\tfrac{1}{2}\omega')</math>; this would give <math>f_1(\tfrac{1}{2}\omega+\tfrac{1}{2}\omega') = 0</math>, while <math>[f_1(\tfrac{1}{2}\omega+\tfrac{1}{2}\omega')]^2 = e_2-e_1</math>. We thus infer that <math>f_1(z+\omega) = f_1(z)</math>, <math>f_1(z+\omega') = -f_1(z)</math>, <math>f_1(z+\omega+\omega') = -f_1(z)</math>. The function <math>f_1(z)</math> is thus doubly periodic with the periods <math>\omega</math> and <math>2\omega'</math>; in a parallelogram of which two sides are <math>\omega</math> and <math>2\omega'</math> it has poles at <math>z=0</math>, <math>z=\omega'</math> each of the first order, and zeros of the first order at <math>z=\tfrac{1}{2}\omega</math>, <math>z=\tfrac{1}{2}\omega+\omega'</math>; it is thus a doubly periodic function of the second order with two different poles of the first order in its parallelogram <math>(\omega, 2\omega')</math>. We may similarly consider the functions <math>f_2(z) = [\wp(z)-e_2]^{\frac{1}{2}}</math>, <math>f_3(z) = [\wp(z)-e_3]^{\frac{1}{2}}</math>; they give
{{block center|<math>f_2(z+\omega+\omega') = f_2(z),\ f_2(z+\omega) = -f_2(z),\ f_2(z+\omega') = -f_2(z),</math>}}
{{block center|<math>f_3(z+\omega') = f_3z,\ f_3(z+\omega) = -f_3(z),\ f_3(z+\omega+\omega') = -f_3(z).</math>}}
Taking <math>u = z(e_1-e_3)^{\frac{1}{2}}</math>, with a definite determination of the constant <math>(e_1-e_3)^{\frac{1}{2}}</math>, it is usual, taking the preliminary signs so that for <math>z=0</math> each of <math>zf_1(z)</math>, <math>zf_2(z)</math>, <math>zf_3(z)</math> is equal to <math>+1</math>, to put
{{block center|<math>\text{sn}(u) = \frac{(e_1-e_3)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{f_3(z)},\ \text{cn}(u) = \frac{f_1(z)}{f_3(z)},\ \text{dn}(u) = \frac{f_2(z)}{f_3(z)},</math>}}
{{block center|<math>k^2 = (e_2-e_3)/(e_1-e_3),\ \text{K} = \tfrac{1}{2}\omega(e_1-e_3)^{\frac{1}{2}},\ i\text{K}' = \tfrac{1}{2}\omega'(e_1-e_3)^{\frac{1}{2}};</math>}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader||FUNCTION|319}}</noinclude>To prove the last of these results, we write, for <math>|z| < |\Omega|</math>,
{{block center|<math>\frac{1}{(z-\Omega)^2} - \frac{1}{\Omega^2} = \frac{2z}{\Omega^3} + \frac{3z^2}{\Omega^4} + \dots,</math>}}
and hence, if <math>\Sigma'\Omega^{-2n} = \sigma_n</math>, since <math>\Sigma'\Omega^{-(2n-1)} = 0</math>, we have, for sufficiently small <math>z</math> greater than zero,
{{block center|<math>f(z) = z^{-2} + 3\sigma_2 . z^2 + 5\sigma_3 . z^4 + \dots</math>}}
and
{{block center|<math>\phi(z) = -2z^{-3} + 6\sigma_2 . z + 20\sigma_3 . z^3 + \dots;</math>}}
using these series we find that the function
{{block center|<math>\text{F}(z) = [\phi(z)]^2 - 4[f(z)]^3 + 60\sigma_2 f(z) + 140\sigma_3</math>}}
contains no negative powers of <math>z</math>, being equal to a power series in <math>z^2</math> beginning with a term in <math>z^2</math>. The function <math>\text{F}(z)</math> is, however, doubly periodic, with periods <math>\omega</math>, <math>\omega'</math>, and can only be infinite when either <math>f(z)</math> or <math>\phi(z)</math> is infinite; this follows from its form in <math>f(z)</math> and <math>\phi(z)</math>; thus in one parallelogram of periods it can be infinite only when <math>z=0</math>; we have proved, however, that it is not infinite, but, on the contrary, vanishes, when <math>z=0</math>. Being, therefore, never infinite for finite values of <math>z</math> it is a constant, and therefore necessarily always zero. Putting therefore <math>f(z) = \zeta</math> and <math>\phi(z) = d\zeta/dz</math> we see that
{{block center|<math>\frac{dz}{d\zeta} = (4\zeta^3 - 60\sigma_2\zeta - 140\sigma_3)^{-\frac{1}{2}}.</math>}}
Historically it was in the discussion of integrals such as
{{block center|<math>\int d\zeta(4\zeta^3 - 60\sigma_2 . \zeta - 140\sigma_3)^{-\frac{1}{2}},</math>}}
regarded as a branch of Integral Calculus, that the doubly periodic functions arose. As in the familiar case
{{block center|<math>z = \int_0^\zeta (1-\zeta^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}} d\zeta,</math>}}
where <math>\zeta = \sin z</math>, it has proved finally to be simpler to regard <math>\zeta</math> as a function of <math>z</math>. We shall come to the other point of view below, under § 20, ''Elliptic Integrals''.

To prove that any doubly periodic function <math>\text{F}(z)</math> with periods <math>\omega</math>, <math>\omega'</math>, having poles at the points <math>z=a_1, \dots z=a_m</math> of a parallelogram, these being, for simplicity of explanation, supposed to be all of the first order, is rationally expressible in terms of <math>\phi(z)</math> and <math>f(z)</math>, and we proceed as follows:—

Consider the expression
{{block center|<math>\Phi(z) = \frac{(\zeta,1)_m + \eta(\zeta,1)_{m-2}}{(\zeta-\text{A}_1)(\zeta-\text{A}_2) \dots (\zeta-\text{A}_m)}</math>}}
where <math>\text{A}_s=f(a_s)</math>, <math>\zeta</math> is an abbreviation for <math>f(z)</math> and <math>\eta</math> for <math>\phi(z)</math>, and <math>(\zeta,1)_m</math>, <math>(\zeta,1)_{m-2}</math>, denote integral polynomials in <math>\zeta</math>, of respective orders <math>m</math> and <math>m-2</math>, so that there are <math>2m</math> unspecified, homogeneously entering, constants in the numerator. It is supposed that no one of the points <math>a_1, \dots a_m</math> is one of the points <math>m\omega+m'\omega'</math> where <math>f(z)=\infty</math>. The function <math>\Phi(z)</math> is a monogenic function of <math>z</math> with the periods <math>\omega</math>, <math>\omega'</math>, becoming infinite (and having singularities) only when (1) <math>\zeta=\infty</math> or (2) one of the factors <math>\zeta-\text{A}_s</math> is zero. In a period parallelogram including <math>z=0</math> the first arises only for <math>z=0</math>; since for <math>\zeta=\infty</math>, <math>\eta</math> is in a finite ratio to <math>\zeta^{3/2}</math>; the function <math>\Phi(z)</math> for <math>\zeta=\infty</math> is not infinite provided the coefficient of <math>\zeta^m</math> in <math>(\zeta,1)_m</math> is not zero; thus <math>\Phi(z)</math> is regular about <math>z=0</math>. When <math>\zeta-\text{A}_s=0</math>, that is <math>f(z)=f(a_s)</math>, we have <math>z=\pm a_s+m\omega+m'\omega'</math>, and no other values of <math>z</math>, <math>m</math> and <math>m'</math> being integers; suppose the unspecified coefficients in the numerator so taken that the numerator vanished to the first order in each of the <math>m</math> points <math>-a_1, -a_2, \dots -a_m</math>; that is, if <math>\phi(a_s)=\text{B}_s</math>, and therefore <math>\phi(-a_s)=-\text{B}_s</math>, so that we have the <math>m</math> relations
{{block center|<math>(\text{A}_s,1)_m - \text{B}_s(\text{A}_s,1)_{m-2}=0;</math>}}
then the function <math>\Phi(z)</math> will only have the <math>m</math> poles <math>a_1, \dots a_m</math>. Denoting further the <math>m</math> zeros of <math>\text{F}(z)</math> by <math>a_1', \dots a_m'</math>, putting <math>f(a_s')=\text{A}_s'</math>, <math>\phi(a_s')=\text{B}_s'</math>, suppose the coefficients of the numerator of <math>\Phi(z)</math> to satisfy the further <math>m-1</math> conditions
{{block center|<math>(\text{A}_s', 1)_m + \text{B}_s'(\text{A}_s',1)_{m-2}=0</math>}} for <math>s=1, 2, \dots (m-1)</math>. The ratios of the <math>2m</math> coefficients in the numerator of <math>\Phi(z)</math> can always be chosen so that the <math>m+(m-1)</math> linear conditions are all satisfied. Consider then the ratio
{{block center|<math>\text{F}(z)/\Phi(z):</math>}}
it is a doubly periodic function with no singularity other than the one pole <math>a_m'</math>. It is therefore a constant, the numerator of <math>\Phi(z)</math> vanishing spontaneously in <math>a_m'</math>. We have
{{block center|<math>\text{F}(z)=\text{A}\Phi(z),</math>}}
where <math>\text{A}</math> is a constant; by which <math>\text{F}(z)</math> is expressed rationally in terms of <math>f(z)</math> and <math>\phi(z)</math>, as was desired.

When <math>z=0</math> is a pole of <math>\text{F}(z)</math>, say of order <math>r</math>, the other poles, each of the first order, being <math>a_1, \dots a_m</math>, similar reasoning can be applied to a function
{{block center|<math>\frac{(\zeta, 1)_h+\eta(\zeta, 1)_k}{(\zeta-\text{A}_1)\dots(\zeta-\text{A}_m)},</math>}}
where <math>h</math>, <math>k</math> are such that the greater of <math>2h-2m</math>, <math>2k+3-2m</math> is equal to <math>r</math>; the case where some of the poles <math>a_1, \dots a_m</math> are multiple is to be met by introducing corresponding multiple factors in the denominator and taking a corresponding numerator. We give a solution of the general problem below, of a different form.

One important application of the result is the theorem that the functions <math>f(z+t)</math>, <math>\phi(z+t)</math>, which are such doubly periodic function of <math>z</math> as have been discussed, can each be expressed, so far as they depend on <math>z</math>, rationally in terms of <math>f(z)</math> and <math>\phi(z)</math>, and therefore, so far as they depend on <math>z</math> and <math>t</math>, rationally in terms of <math>f(z)</math>, <math>f(t)</math>, <math>\phi(z)</math> and <math>\phi(t)</math>. It can in fact be shown, by reasoning analogous to that given above, that
{{block center|<math>f(z+t)+f(z)+f(t) = \tfrac{1}{4}\left[\frac{\phi(z)-\phi(t)}{f(z)-f(t)}\right]^2</math>.}}

This shows that if <math>\text{F}(z)</math> be any single valued monogenic function which is doubly periodic and of meromorphic character, then <math>\text{F}(z+t)</math> is an algebraic function of <math>\text{F}(z)</math> and <math>\text{F}(t)</math>. Conversely any single valued monogenic function of meromorphic character, <math>\text{F}(z)</math>, which is such that <math>\text{F}(z+t)</math> is an algebraic function of <math>\text{F}(z)</math> and <math>\text{F}(t)</math>, can be shown to be a doubly periodic function, or a function obtained from such by degeneration (in virtue of special relations connecting the fundamental constants).

The functions <math>f(z)</math>, <math>\phi(z)</math> above are usually denoted by <math>\mathfrak{P}(z)</math>, <math>\mathfrak{P}'(z)</math>; further the fundamental differential equation is usually written
{{block center|<math>(\mathfrak{P}'z)^2 = 4(\mathfrak{P}z)^3-g_2\mathfrak{P}z-g_3</math>,}}
and the roots of the cubic on the right are denoted by <math>e_1</math>, <math>e_2</math>, <math>e_3</math>; for the odd function, <math>\mathfrak{P}'z</math>, we have, for the congruent arguments <math>-\tfrac{1}{2}\omega</math> and <math>\tfrac{1}{2}\omega</math>, <math>\mathfrak{P}'(\tfrac{1}{2}\omega) = -\mathfrak{P}'(-\tfrac{1}{2}\omega) = -\mathfrak{P}'(\tfrac{1}{2}\omega)</math>, and hence <math>\mathfrak{P}'(\tfrac{1}{2}\omega) = 0</math>; hence we can take <math>e_1 = \mathfrak{P}(\tfrac{1}{2}\omega)</math>, <math>e_2 = \mathfrak{P}(\tfrac{1}{2}\omega+\tfrac{1}{2}\omega')</math>, <math>e_3 = \mathfrak{P}(\tfrac{1}{2}\omega')</math>. It can then be proved that <math>[\mathfrak{P}(z)-e_1][\mathfrak{P}(z+\tfrac{1}{2}\omega)-e_1] = (e_1-e_2)(e_1-e_3)</math>, with similar equations for the other half periods. Consider more particularly the function <math>\mathfrak{P}(z)-e_1</math>; like <math>\mathfrak{P}(z)</math> it has a pole of the second order at <math>z=0</math>, its expansion in its neighbourhood being of the form <math>z^{-2}(1-e_1z^2+\text{A}z^4+\dots)</math>; having no other pole, it has therefore either two zeros, or a double zero in a period parallelogram <math>(\omega, \omega')</math>. In fact near its zero <math>\tfrac{1}{2}\omega</math> its expansion is <math>(x-\tfrac{1}{2}\omega)\mathfrak{P}'(\tfrac{1}{2}\omega)+\tfrac{1}{2}(z-\tfrac{1}{2}\omega)^2\mathfrak{P}''(\tfrac{1}{2}\omega)+\dots</math>; we have seen that <math>\mathfrak{P}'(\tfrac{1}{2}\omega) = 0</math>; thus it has a zero of the second order wherever it vanishes. Thus it appears that the square root <math>[\wp(z)-e_1]^{\frac{1}{2}}</math>, if we attach a definite sign to it for some particular value of <math>z</math>, is a single valued function of <math>z</math>; for it can at most have two values, and the only small circuits in the plane which could lead to an interchange of these values are those about either a pole or a zero, neither of which, as we have seen, has this effect; the function is therefore single valued for any circuit. Denoting the function, for a moment, by <math>f_1(z)</math>, we have <math>f_1(z+\omega) = \pm f_1(z)</math>, <math>f_1(z+\omega') = \pm f_1(z)</math>; it can be seen by considerations of continuity that the right sign in either of these equations does not vary with <math>z</math>; not both these signs can be positive, since the function has only one pole, of the first order, in a parallelogram <math>(\omega, \omega')</math>; from the expansion of <math>f_1(z)</math> about <math>z=0</math>, namely <math>z^{-1}(1-\tfrac{1}{2}e_1z^2+\dots)</math>, it follows that <math>f_1(z)</math> is an odd function, and hence <math>f_1(-\tfrac{1}{2}\omega') = -f_1(\tfrac{1}{2}\omega')</math>, which is not zero since <math>[f_1(\tfrac{1}{2}\omega')]^2 = e_3-e_1</math>, so that we have <math>f_1(z+\omega') = -f_1(z)</math>; an equation <math>f_1(z+\omega) = -f_1(z)</math> would then give <math>f_1(z+\omega+\omega') = f_1(z)</math>, and hence <math>f_1(\tfrac{1}{2}\omega+\tfrac{1}{2}\omega') = f_1(-\tfrac{1}{2}\omega-\tfrac{1}{2}\omega')</math>, of which the latter is <math>-f_1(\tfrac{1}{2}\omega+\tfrac{1}{2}\omega')</math>; this would give <math>f_1(\tfrac{1}{2}\omega+\tfrac{1}{2}\omega') = 0</math>, while <math>[f_1(\tfrac{1}{2}\omega+\tfrac{1}{2}\omega')]^2 = e_2-e_1</math>. We thus infer that <math>f_1(z+\omega) = f_1(z)</math>, <math>f_1(z+\omega') = -f_1(z)</math>, <math>f_1(z+\omega+\omega') = -f_1(z)</math>. The function <math>f_1(z)</math> is thus doubly periodic with the periods <math>\omega</math> and <math>2\omega'</math>; in a parallelogram of which two sides are <math>\omega</math> and <math>2\omega'</math> it has poles at <math>z=0</math>, <math>z=\omega'</math> each of the first order, and zeros of the first order at <math>z=\tfrac{1}{2}\omega</math>, <math>z=\tfrac{1}{2}\omega+\omega'</math>; it is thus a doubly periodic function of the second order with two different poles of the first order in its parallelogram <math>(\omega, 2\omega')</math>. We may similarly consider the functions <math>f_2(z) = [\wp(z)-e_2]^{\frac{1}{2}}</math>, <math>f_3(z) = [\wp(z)-e_3]^{\frac{1}{2}}</math>; they give
{{block center|<math>f_2(z+\omega+\omega') = f_2(z),\ f_2(z+\omega) = -f_2(z),\ f_2(z+\omega') = -f_2(z),</math>}}
{{block center|<math>f_3(z+\omega') = f_3z,\ f_3(z+\omega) = -f_3(z),\ f_3(z+\omega+\omega') = -f_3(z).</math>}}
Taking <math>u = z(e_1-e_3)^{\frac{1}{2}}</math>, with a definite determination of the constant <math>(e_1-e_3)^{\frac{1}{2}}</math>, it is usual, taking the preliminary signs so that for <math>z=0</math> each of <math>zf_1(z)</math>, <math>zf_2(z)</math>, <math>zf_3(z)</math> is equal to <math>+1</math>, to put
{{block center|<math>\text{sn}(u) = \frac{(e_1-e_3)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{f_3(z)},\ \text{cn}(u) = \frac{f_1(z)}{f_3(z)},\ \text{dn}(u) = \frac{f_2(z)}{f_3(z)},</math>}}
{{block center|<math>k^2 = (e_2-e_3)/(e_1-e_3),\ \text{K} = \tfrac{1}{2}\omega(e_1-e_3)^{\frac{1}{2}},\ i\text{K}' = \tfrac{1}{2}\omega'(e_1-e_3)^{\frac{1}{2}};</math>}} thus <math>\operatorname{sn}(u)</math> is an odd doubly periodic function of the second order with the periods <math>4\text{K}</math>, <math>2i\text{K}</math>, having poles of the first order at <math>u=i\text{K}'</math>, <math>u=2\text{K}+i\text{K}'</math>, and zeros of the first order at <math>u=0</math>, <math>u=2\text{K}</math>; similarly <math>\operatorname{cn}(u)</math>, <math>\operatorname{dn}(u)</math>are even doubly periodic functions whose periods can be written down, and <math>\operatorname{sn}^2(u)+\operatorname{cn}^2(u)=1</math>, <math>k^2\operatorname{sn}^2(u)+\operatorname{dn}^2(u)=1</math>; if <math>x=\operatorname{sn}(u)</math> we at once find, from the relations given here, that
{{block center|<math>\frac{du}{dx}=[(1-x^2)(1-k^2x^2)]^{-\frac{1}{2}};</math>}}
if we put <math>x=\sin\phi</math> we have
{{block center|<math>\frac{du}{d\phi}=[1-k^2\sin^2\phi]^{-\frac{1}{2}},</math>}}
and if we call <math>\phi</math> the amplitude of <math>u</math>, we may write <math>\phi=\operatorname{am}(u)</math>, <math>x=\sin.\operatorname{am}(u)</math>, which explains the origin of the notation <math>\operatorname{sn}(u)</math>. Similarly <math>\operatorname{cn}(u)</math> is an abbreviation of <math>\cos.\operatorname{am}(u)</math>, and <math>\operatorname{dn}(u)</math> of <math>\Delta\operatorname{am}(u)</math>, where <math>\Delta(\phi)</math> meant <math>(1-k^2\sin^2\phi)^{\frac{1}{2}}</math>. The addition equation for each of the functions <math>f_1(z)</math>, <math>f_2(z)</math>, <math>f_3(z)</math> is very simple, being
{{block center|<math>f(z+t)=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial z}+\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\right)\log\frac{f(z)+f(t)}{f(z)-f(t)}=\frac{f(z)f'(t)-f(t)f'(z)}{f^2(z)-f^2(t)},</math>}}
where <math>f_1'(z)</math> means <math>df_1(z)/dz</math>, which is equal to <math>-f_2(z).f_3(z)</math>, and <math>f^2(z)</math><noinclude><references/></noinclude>
